companion.title: Why a Metal Spoon Feels Colder
companion.subtitle: Conduction, temperature versus sensation, and the direction of heat transfer

chapters.title: Sensation Is Not a Thermometer
chapters.goal: Explain why two objects at the same temperature can feel different.

claims.text: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon at the same room temperature can still feel different to the touch.
claims.reason: cue-1 states both spoons can be at the same room temperature and still feel different.

claims.text: The metal usually feels colder because it moves thermal energy away from a warmer hand more quickly.
claims.reason: cue-1 gives the faster-transfer explanation; cue-5 links sensation to rate of energy transfer.

claims.text: Concluding that the metal must be colder simply because it feels colder is not justified.
claims.reason: cue-5 explicitly says the student's conclusion is not justified.

claims.text: A suitable thermometer, not touch, is the way to test whether the two objects' temperatures actually differ.
claims.reason: cue-5 recommends comparing with a suitable thermometer; cue-1 says feeling cold does not measure temperature.

checks.concept: Why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one at the same temperature
checks.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have sat in the same room for hours. Why does the metal one feel colder?

choices.text: The metal is actually at a lower temperature than the wood.
choices.explanation: Misconception: the source says both can be at the same room temperature and that feeling cold does not measure temperature.

choices.text: The metal transfers thermal energy away from the hand more quickly.
choices.explanation: Correct: the sensation depends on the rate of energy transfer, and metal conducts quickly.

choices.text: Cold from the metal flows into the hand.
choices.explanation: Misconception: energy flows from the hotter hand to the colder spoon; cold is not a substance that enters the hand.

recovery.question: A student insists the metal spoon is colder because it feels colder. What is the best response?

choices.text: Agree, because touch reliably reports temperature.
Explain that touch reflects the rate of energy transfer, so measure both with a thermometer instead.
Say the wooden spoon must be warmer because wood stores more heat.

recovery.explanation: The sensation depends on how fast energy leaves the hand, not temperature alone; a thermometer settles the question.

chapters.title: Conduction and Conductors
chapters.goal: Describe thermal conduction and why metals and wood behave differently.

claims.text: Thermal conduction transfers energy through matter without the bulk movement of the material itself.
claims.reason: Definition matches cue-2 verbatim in substance.

claims.text: Metals are often good thermal conductors, while wood generally conducts heat much more slowly.
claims.reason: cue-2 states metals are often good conductors and wood conducts much more slowly.

claims.text: Because wood conducts slowly, a wooden spoon handle can stay comfortable longer when part of the spoon is in hot liquid.
claims.reason: cue-2 gives this handle example directly.

claims.text: An insulating glove reduces heat transfer between a hand and an object but does not create heat.
claims.reason: cue-6 states the glove reduces transfer and does not create heat.

checks.concept: Why a wooden handle stays comfortable when the spoon is in hot liquid
checks.question: Part of a wooden spoon sits in hot soup. Why can its handle stay comfortable to hold longer than a metal one would?

choices.text: Wood conducts heat much more slowly than metal.
choices.explanation: Correct: slow conduction delays energy reaching the handle.

choices.text: Wood absorbs the heat and destroys it.
choices.explanation: Misconception: energy is transferred, not destroyed; insulators only slow exchange.

choices.text: Wood stays at the soup's temperature but feels cool anyway.
choices.explanation: Misconception: the point is that heat reaches the handle slowly, not that a hot handle feels cool.

recovery.question: Which property of wood explains why a wooden handle heats up slowly when the other end is hot?

choices.text: It is a poor thermal conductor.
It is a good thermal conductor.

recovery.explanation: Wood conducts heat slowly, so energy takes longer to travel along the handle.

chapters.title: Direction of Heat and Equilibrium
chapters.goal: Clarify how energy flows between objects and how temperature differs from thermal energy.

claims.text: Energy transfers spontaneously from a hotter object to a colder one when they can exchange heat.
Heat does not flow because cold is a substance entering the warm object.
claims.reason: cue-4 rejects cold as a substance entering the warm object.

claims.text: At thermal equilibrium there is no net heat transfer between two objects.
claims.reason: cue-4 states no net heat transfer at thermal equilibrium.

claims.text: Temperature describes a thermal state, whereas total internal energy also depends on the amount of material and its properties.
A larger amount of water can hold more internal energy than a smaller amount at the same temperature.

checks.concept: Direction of spontaneous heat transfer between a hand and a cooler spoon
checks.question: When a warm hand touches a cooler metal spoon, what happens?

choices.text: Cold flows from the spoon into the hand.
choices.explanation: Misconception: cold is not a substance that flows; energy moves from hot to cold.

choices.text: Energy transfers from the hand to the spoon.
choices.explanation: Correct: energy spontaneously moves from the hotter hand to the colder spoon.

choices.text: No energy moves because they are already in equilibrium.
choices.explanation: Misconception: equilibrium only exists once temperatures are equal; a warmer hand and cooler spoon are not yet in equilibrium.

recovery.question: Two objects at different temperatures can exchange heat. In which direction does energy spontaneously move?

choices.text: From the colder object to the hotter object.
From the hotter object to the colder object.
Equally in both directions at all times.

recovery.explanation: Energy flows spontaneously from hotter to colder until thermal equilibrium, when net transfer stops.

glossary.definition: Transfer of energy through matter without bulk movement of the material.
The state in which two objects have no net heat transfer between them.
A material, such as a glove, that reduces heat transfer without creating heat.

run.reviewer: Model support review; not independent factual verification
